style: Product first, founder spoken language, no backstory, no long dashes. Sources and unverified claims belong in notes. Audience-specific purpose and concrete mechanism. No fabricated customer results.

pitches.title: Explain A Story in 30 seconds
pitches.body: A Story is an AI biographer that interviews your parents by phone and keeps their stories in their own voice. You set it up; they answer the call. The interviewer remembers earlier conversations, so it can return to a person or a photograph they mentioned. Relatives add their memories too. We're building a family history that keeps growing as the family does.
pitches.notes:
Aim: make the product easy to repeat to someone else.
Lead with the phone interview, not an abstract archive. Keep the family-context loop to one sentence.
Use the 1-minute version if they ask how it works. This describes the intended product experience; confirm which parts are live before demonstrating.

pitches.title: 30 seconds with an investor
pitches.body: We're building A Story, an AI biographer that calls your parents and records their stories. The buyer is the adult child who wants those stories but keeps putting off the work of interviewing and organizing them. Families pay for guided interviews; relatives contribute context that makes the next call more useful. Our bet is that a memoir gift can become a service families keep using.
pitches.notes:
Aim: earn the next question, not explain the whole company.
Buyer: adult child. User: willing parent or grandparent. Commercial bet: repeat interviews, rather than relying only on a finished book.
Recurring use is a thesis, not measured retention. Have current usage and paid-demand evidence ready before a serious investor meeting.

pitches.title: When a family asks how it works
pitches.body: A Story helps you record your parents' stories without turning it into another project you have to manage. You choose a time for a phone interview. They answer and talk, and an AI interviewer asks follow-up questions. We're building it to remember earlier conversations, so your dad can pick up the story about his first job without starting from the beginning. The recording stays in his voice, alongside a transcript and the photographs your family adds. Suppose he mentions an old neighbor. You might have a photo of them that he hasn't seen in years. That gives the next conversation somewhere to start. You can turn selected stories into a book, but you can keep adding to the family record afterward. Who would you want to start with?
pitches.notes:
Aim: help the family picture the first interview and name a willing storyteller.
Use one ordinary example, then ask a real question. Pause after the last sentence and listen.
The neighbor/photo example is illustrative. Do not present it as a customer result. Verify availability, consent workflow and current pricing before offering a purchase.

pitches.title: Invite a parent or grandparent
pitches.body: We're making A Story to help families hear the stories they haven't asked about yet. You don't need to write a memoir or prepare a speech. The idea is to arrange a phone call, let you talk about something you remember, and have an AI interviewer follow the conversation. It might ask about your first job, someone in an old photograph, or a place you used to live. It keeps your voice, so your family can hear you telling the story yourself. Later, they can add photographs or their own memories. Before we try a call, we'll explain what's recorded and who can see it. Is there a story you enjoy telling that your family hasn't heard?
pitches.notes:
Aim: invite participation without pressure.
Say explicitly that the interviewer is AI. Keep the invitation conversational, and do not assume the adult child can consent for the storyteller.
Explain the actual recording, sharing and deletion controls before any trial. This is an invitation draft, not an approved service or privacy promise.

pitches.title: Propose a community pilot
pitches.body: A Story is an AI biographer that helps families record a parent's stories through phone interviews. I'd like to explore a small pilot with families in your community. A relative would help set it up, the storyteller would answer scheduled calls, and the family could add photographs and memories afterward. For your organization, the question is whether this gives families something useful without adding a new job for your staff. We'd agree on consent, access and responsibilities before starting. We'd measure whether storytellers complete a second interview, whether relatives contribute, and how much help families need. If that works, we can discuss a larger program. Who on your team would be best placed to help us design the first test?
pitches.notes:
Aim: get a pilot-design conversation with the right person.
Offer a scoped test, not an unconfirmed institutional partnership. Ask about staff time and family needs before discussing distribution.
No organization has agreed to this pilot through this pitch. Define permission, responsibilities, pricing and measures together before making commitments.

pitches.title: Make the case for voice credits
pitches.body: We're building A Story, an AI biographer that interviews parents and grandparents by phone. The hard part is the follow-up. A storyteller might mention a name in passing, hesitate over a date, or leave a story unfinished. The interviewer needs to listen, use what the family has already shared, and ask the next useful question without making the call feel scripted. We'd use your startup credits to test voice quality, response delay and transcription on that interview task. We'd also measure cost per completed interview, because a family product has to remain affordable when people keep using it. We can show the interview flow and propose a bounded comparison with our current approach. What does your program need to evaluate that use case?
pitches.notes:
Aim: tie credits to a concrete workload and a useful evaluation.
Bring an actual interview demo and a short benchmark plan. Confirm the current provider stack rather than saying an explored provider is deployed.
Request a controlled trial. Check data use, overages, renewal and publicity obligations before accepting program terms.

pitches.title: Three-minute competition pitch
pitches.body: A Story is an AI biographer that interviews your parents by phone and preserves their stories in their own voice. Our first customer is the adult child who keeps meaning to ask more about a parent's life. They might speak every week and still know almost nothing about the years before they were born. The problem is the work between wanting those stories and recording them: arranging a conversation, knowing what to ask, following up, and keeping everything somewhere the family can find it. We're building A Story to do that work through a familiar phone call. A relative sets it up. The parent answers and talks. The interviewer follows what they say and uses earlier conversations to ask better questions. The original recording stays alongside the transcript, photographs and family contributions. Here's an example of the experience we're building. Your mother describes an old photograph and mentions a friend you've never heard of. Her brother adds the friend's name and remembers why they were there. That becomes a question for a later interview. Each person's account stays attached to the person who told it, including when they remember the same day differently. That loop is the reason this can be more than a one-time recording. Family contributions give the next interview a reason to happen, and each interview gives the family more to respond to. People already buy memoir gifts. We want to earn that same first purchase and then give the family a reason to keep going. Our business model charges for guided interview time, with books as an additional purchase. We are bootstrapped, with a four-person team based in Michigan. The immediate work is to establish paid demand, repeat interviews and the actual cost of serving a family. Those are the results we want this program to help us reach. We would use support to improve call reliability and test one gifting channel, measuring the path from purchase to a first interview and then a second. A Story starts with a practical invitation: answer the phone and tell us what happened. The family can keep asking from there.
pitches.notes:
Aim: judges should leave knowing the buyer, the experience, the repeat-use bet and what support would prove.
Deliver as one connected argument. No founder backstory, speculative market total or invented traction. The photo/friend sequence is a product illustration.
Before using: confirm live capabilities; replace the general support request with this competition's actual award and a budget. Bring real completed-call and paid-demand evidence if available. Four-person team, bootstrapped and Michigan are owner-confirmed.

pitches.title: Three-minute application video
pitches.body: I'm Bao Vo, co-founder and COO of A Story. We're building an AI biographer that interviews parents and grandparents by phone and records their stories in their own voice. The first person we're building for is the adult child who wants to capture a parent's life but hasn't found a way to make it happen consistently. Asking once is easy. Keeping track of people, photographs and unfinished stories takes work, and that work usually belongs to one person in the family. A Story starts with a scheduled phone call. The parent talks; the interviewer listens and asks follow-up questions. Earlier conversations and family contributions give it context for the next interview. Think about a photograph your mother describes. Her brother might remember who was there; another relative might have the photograph itself. We want those pieces connected to the story, with each account attributed to its source. They can become the starting point for another call. The original voice remains part of the record, so relatives can hear the person telling it rather than only read a rewritten chapter. Families can make a keepsake book when they want one and continue adding to the archive afterward. Our commercial bet is that the same gift that starts a memoir can start an ongoing interview service. Families pay for guided calls, while relatives' contributions help create a reason for another interview. We don't need everyone in the family to buy a separate subscription for that loop to work. We are a bootstrapped four-person team in Michigan, founded in June 2026. Our next job is to establish whether families will pay, whether storytellers return for a second interview, and whether we can deliver those calls reliably at a cost that supports the business. We want to use this program to improve that experience and test a focused gifting channel. We would judge progress by paid families and completed repeat interviews, not by how many people say the idea sounds nice. A Story gives a family a way to begin the conversations they keep putting off, and a record they can keep building together.
pitches.notes:
Aim: explain the business plainly to the camera.
Confirm the program's presenter rules, video length and whether a demo is allowed. Bao's role, team size, bootstrapped status, location and founding month are confirmed.
Add a current product demonstration or dated pilot evidence only if verified. This is a three-minute competition draft; it is not the one-minute YC founder-video format. Use your own delivery rather than reading mechanically.

pitches.title: Five-minute investor pitch
pitches.body: We're building A Story, an AI biographer that calls your parents and records their stories. The customer we're starting with is an adult child buying for a willing parent or grandparent. They want the stories, but interviewing a parent, asking good follow-ups and organizing everything is a project they keep putting off. A Story makes the first step a phone call. The relative sets it up; the parent answers and talks. We're building an interviewer that remembers earlier conversations and uses the family's contributions to decide what to ask next. The voice recording remains alongside the transcript and the photographs, people and places in the story. Suppose your mother describes a photograph from her first job. Her brother recognizes someone in it and adds a name. That gives the next interview a specific question to ask. If they remember the day differently, their accounts stay attributed to them. We don't need to pick one version and erase the other. This example explains the product loop: an interview prompts a family contribution, and that contribution creates a reason for another interview. The commercial opportunity starts with a purchase people already understand, a gift that helps a parent tell their life story. The bigger question is what happens after the first set of stories. We want the family to keep using A Story because the next conversation is worth having. A printed book can be part of that experience without being the end of it. Families pay for guided interview time; relatives can participate in the shared record. That puts the recurring service where both the cost and the value are: the conversation itself. We need to earn repeat use, not assume that putting a subscription on a memoir creates it. That also shapes how we think about acquisition. The first test is a gifting occasion with a clear buyer and a willing storyteller. We want to follow the same family from purchase to the first completed interview and then to a second. If the buyer pays but the parent never answers, we haven't solved the problem. If interviews happen but the family never returns to the stories, the archive isn't earning its place either. We would measure those behaviors before widening the audience or adding more acquisition channels. Our proposed advantage is the context accumulated by the family: earlier conversations, photographs, relationships and questions still worth asking. That context only matters if it makes the next interview better. We would demonstrate it with a follow-up that depends on something already shared, then measure whether families return. A competitor can add an interview feature. We have to build a product families choose to keep contributing to. The economics deserve the same discipline. We need to measure voice usage, response delay, support time and cost per completed interview against actual paid usage. Headline AI credits may help us experiment, but they do not replace sustainable delivery costs. We are a bootstrapped, four-person team based in Michigan. At this stage, the most useful investor conversation is about the evidence needed to make this a durable consumer business: paid demand, repeat calls, family participation and acquisition cost in a real cohort. I'd like to show you the interview experience and discuss which of those results you would need to see before a follow-up investment conversation.
pitches.notes:
Aim: make the investor evaluate a specific consumer-business loop.
Order: product and buyer, one illustrative experience, recurring value, distribution, defensibility test, economics, next conversation.
This is a product and business thesis, not a traction update. Add current revenue, paid families, repeat-call evidence and an approved raise amount before turning this into a fundraising ask. No unsupported TAM, retention, launch or customer-count claim is used.

pitches.title: Seven-minute family product demonstration
pitches.body:
OPEN - 1 minute
A Story helps you record a parent's stories through phone interviews. You help set it up; they answer and talk. The family record can include their original voice, photographs and memories from other relatives. I'd like to show you one conversation and what the family can do with it afterward.

INTERVIEW - 2 minutes
Play a permissioned recording or use the working product to demonstrate a short interview. If it is a prepared example, introduce it as an example before playing it. Show a follow-up tied to something the storyteller just said. Let the conversation do the explaining.

AFTER THE CALL - 1 minute
This is where the interview belongs in the family record. Start with the voice recording, then show how the transcript and any photograph relate to it. If a screen or behavior is still a prototype, say that once, at the point where you show it.

FAMILY CONTEXT - 1 minute
A parent may mention a person another relative recognizes. Show how you would attach that relative's contribution and use it to prepare a later question. Explain which parts work today and which are being built. The example is a demonstration, not evidence of a customer's behavior.

THE FAMILY'S QUESTIONS - 2 minutes
Who would you want to interview? What would make them comfortable trying a call? What would you want to hear again afterward? Listen before offering a next step. Explain the actual recording and sharing controls. Close with a trial only if one is available and the storyteller is willing.
pitches.notes:
Aim: let a family evaluate the experience, not sit through a seven-minute sales speech.
Timing: 2 minutes of interview, 2 minutes of explanation, 1 minute of family context, 2 minutes of questions.
Prepare actual screens and permissioned audio in advance. Show consent/access controls only as implemented. The seven-minute target includes the demonstration and discussion; it is not seven minutes of spoken copy.

pitches.title: Ten-minute voice / AI partner briefing
pitches.body:
PRODUCT - 1 minute
A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. Our core experience is a phone interview with a parent or grandparent. We want an interviewer that can use earlier conversations and family context to ask a useful follow-up without interrupting the storyteller's rhythm.

SHOW THE INTERVIEW - 2 minutes
Demonstrate one current conversation. Focus on the transition between listening and asking, then a follow-up grounded in a previous detail. Clearly introduce prepared examples. Explain the actual current integration rather than naming providers we have only explored.

WHAT WE WOULD TEST TOGETHER - 2 minutes
We would compare the same interview task across voice options: response delay, handling of interruptions, transcription of family names and places, follow-up quality and cost per completed interview. Define the test recordings, permissions and measurement method before comparing results. Ask which limits or implementation choices might affect this workload.

CONTEXT AND CONTROL - 2 minutes
The interview and memory system should control which family information reaches a conversation. We want the voice or visual layer to express the interviewer without deciding what is true about the family. Discuss what data the integration needs, how long the provider keeps it and which controls apply to the specific service we would use.

OPTIONAL VISUAL INTERVIEWER - 2 minutes
For web and mobile, we want to explore a visual interviewer that feels personal to a family. Appearance, personality and voice could suit the interview purpose. The same family context would guide its questions. Phone calls remain the simplest core experience. Describe this as an exploration unless a working integration is demonstrated.

REQUEST - 1 minute
We'd like startup support for a bounded evaluation of this interview use case. Credits would let us test the product before choosing an ongoing provider. Technical support would help us understand the latency, usage limits and data controls. Agree on the next technical review and confirm the actual program terms before committing.
pitches.notes:
Aim: get a technical evaluation and a concrete credit/support path.
Prepare: actual stack, consented sample workload, test method, volume estimate and cost baseline. Explored tools are not production integrations.
The ten-minute slot includes a demo and partner questions. For Runway, use the separate avatar exploration wording; do not claim GWM Avatars are already deployed. Payment, overage, retention, publicity and terms require review.

pitches.title: Fifteen-minute competition finals session
pitches.body:
OPEN AND BUYER - 2 minutes
A Story is an AI biographer that interviews your parents by phone and records their stories in their own voice. We start with an adult child who wants to preserve a parent's life but keeps postponing the work. Talking is familiar to the parent. The work of starting, following up and organizing is what we want the product to take on. Explain the first purchase as a family gift, with a willing storyteller at the center.

PRODUCT DEMONSTRATION - 3 minutes
Show an actual interview and one useful follow-up. Then show where the voice recording lives in the family record. Introduce prepared examples as examples. Only demonstrate release features as released. A photograph and a relative's contribution should make the connection to a later question visible.

THE REPEAT-USE BET - 2 minutes
The next question is what makes the family return. A relative recognizes a name, adds a photograph, or remembers an event differently. That supplies context for another conversation. Each contribution stays attached to its source. The commercial bet is that these contributions give the interview service a reason to continue after a first book. We need to prove that behavior with families rather than assume it.

CURRENT EVIDENCE - 2 minutes
Present dated evidence of the product, completed interviews, paid demand and any repeat use. Separate a lead, an interested family and a paying customer. If a measure is not available, name the test that will establish it. Use the evidence gathered before the event; this session plan does not supply or imply traction.

BUSINESS AND FIRST CHANNEL - 2 minutes
Families pay for guided interview time; books are an additional purchase. Explain the current approved offer, actual call usage and delivery cost. Choose one gifting channel and follow the family from purchase through first and second interviews. A partnership discussion is not a distribution agreement, and modeled costs are not observed margins.

WHY THIS APPROACH - 2 minutes
Families have existing ways to record stories. Compare the nearest alternatives on the specific task you just demonstrated: continuity across calls and family context informing the next question. Explain why that behavior matters to the buyer. Avoid claiming that every competitor produces only a one-time book.

THE PROGRAM REQUEST AND CLOSE - 2 minutes
Tie this program's actual support to call reliability, a focused gifting test and measured repeat interviews. State the approved request and spending plan. Return to the product: a parent answers the phone, tells the story, and the family has somewhere to keep asking. Finish inside the slot and leave the event's separate Q&A time available.
pitches.notes:
Aim: show the product and defend the business with real evidence.
This is a 15-minute event plan including demo/evidence presentation, not a finished 15-minute monologue. The 3- and 5-minute scripts provide the core spoken argument.
Evidence to prepare: working demo, permissions, release status, paid/use logs, current pricing, real cost data and a program-specific budget. Do not substitute the old deck's targets for results. Confirm current competition timing separately.

pitches.title: Twenty-minute investor working session
pitches.body:
PRODUCT AND CUSTOMER - 2 minutes
We're building A Story, an AI biographer that calls your parents and records their stories. Our starting customer is the adult child buying for a willing parent or grandparent. The product takes on the repeated interviewing and organizing work. Explain the buyer and storyteller as two people with different needs.

WORKING DEMO - 4 minutes
Show the actual interview experience and the family record. Make one follow-up dependent on context already shared. Explain the current product boundary plainly. A prepared conversation is an example; a production feature is something the investor can see working. Let them interrupt with questions.

PAID DEMAND AND REPEAT USE - 3 minutes
Present current dated evidence. Distinguish leads from paying families and first interviews from repeat use. Explain the friction you observed and what changed in the product. If these data are not yet available, frame the conversation around the test and the result that would change your mind.

BUSINESS MODEL AND COST - 3 minutes
Families pay for guided interview time. Relatives' contributions create context and books are an additional purchase. Use current approved prices and actual cost observations, or identify a cost model as a model. Discuss usage, support and acquisition in the same cohort. Credits help fund tests; expiring credits are not a durable margin advantage.

DISTRIBUTION - 2 minutes
Choose one initial gifting occasion and channel. Show the path from reaching the adult child to a willing storyteller completing two interviews. Name actual agreements only when they exist. Discuss whether the family contribution loop might generate referrals as a hypothesis to measure.

DIFFERENTIATION - 2 minutes
The proposed edge is a family record that supplies context for better subsequent interviews. Demonstrate the mechanism and compare the closest alternatives fairly. Accumulated data matters when it helps the user, not merely because we possess it. Discuss what would make a family stay, contribute and pay again.

FINANCING AND NEXT RESULT - 2 minutes
Present a financing request only after the amount, budget and runway are agreed. Map it to product reliability, paid demand and repeat use. Explain which evidence an investor should expect before the next conversation. A Story is bootstrapped with a four-person Michigan team; do not fill the missing financial details from an old deck.

DISCUSSION - 2 minutes
Which assumption is hardest to believe after seeing the product? Discuss that assumption directly and agree on the next review. Leave the meeting with a specific result to produce, rather than a vague invitation to stay in touch.
pitches.notes:
Aim: run an investor conversation around the product and evidence.
20 minutes = demo, discussion and a short business argument. This is intentionally a meeting plan; use the 5-minute script for uninterrupted speaking.
Have a verified evidence packet and approved financing request. The agent cannot manufacture a customer proof point, margin, growth rate or investment commitment.

pitches.title: YC founder video - one-minute talking points
pitches.body:
Daniel: introduce yourself as co-founder and CEO. Bao: introduce yourself as co-founder and COO.

Explain it in your own words: we're building A Story, an AI biographer that calls your parents and records their stories.

Name the customer: the adult child who wants a parent's stories but keeps putting off the interviewing and organizing.

Explain the insight: a relative's photo or memory gives the next interview a better question. We want that loop to make this a service a family keeps using.

Give one concrete current product or customer result you can substantiate. If there is no customer result yet, state the actual build status.

End with what you are working on next.
pitches.notes:
Aim: show both founders explaining their own business naturally.
YC explicitly asks founders not to recite a prewritten script. Use these as preparation points, then put them away while filming. Both founders should appear. https://www.ycombinator.com/video.html
The video needs a current build/result sentence from you. No traction or founder origin is invented. This is preparation, not a YC-ready certification.

pitches.title: Runway - personalized interviewer exploration
pitches.body: A Story is an ongoing AI biographer for families. We want to explore GWM Avatars as a visual extension of our AI interviewer for web and mobile. A family could talk to a personalized interviewer that remembers earlier conversations and family context, while our existing interview and memory system controls what it knows and asks. We are especially interested in custom voices and expressive real-time conversation. An interviewer could be adapted to the person speaking, the purpose of the interview, and the family's preferences. We'd start with a small evaluation of the conversation experience and cost. Phone calls remain our simplest core experience; avatars could later support onboarding, video interviews and reviewing the family's recorded stories.
pitches.notes:
Aim: explain exactly why Runway could matter to A Story.
This is the owner's proposed exploration, not a claim of a deployed Runway integration. Keep it one paragraph, with ordinary punctuation.
Use a provider-specific demo/test plan and verify program benefits and current questions separately. An application still requires your exact emailed preview and confirmation.
